item.title: Medellín Property Management: The Complete Guide for Owners
item.description: What Medellín property management covers: Airbnb vs long-term rentals, RNT and Law 820 rules, managing from abroad and how to choose a manager (Nov 2026).
item.content:encoded:
Owning an apartment in Medellín, Colombia, is the easy part. Keeping it rented, legal, well maintained and profitable, especially if you live in another country, is where most of the work is. This guide explains what Medellín property management actually covers, the two main ways to rent out a property (short-term and long-term), the rules that apply to each as of November 2026, and how to choose a manager you can trust.

It is written for owners and investors in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta, whether you already own or are still shopping. It is general information, not legal or tax advice, and regulations change, so confirm the current rules for your property with us before you act.

What does a property manager in Medellín do?

A good manager takes over the day-to-day running of the property so the owner does not have to be in the city. Depending on the type of rental, that usually includes:

  • Getting the property ready. Furnishing and equipping an empty unit, professional photos, and a listing or advertisement that matches the property.
  • Finding guests or tenants. Publishing on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO for short stays, or screening tenants for a long-term lease.
  • Pricing. Adjusting nightly rates for season, events and demand, or setting a monthly rent that fits the market and the law.
  • Communication. Answering guests around the clock, or being the tenant's single point of contact.
  • Cleaning and maintenance. Turnovers between stays, inspections, repairs and coordination with the building administration.
  • Compliance. Registrations and reports required by Colombian authorities (more on this below).
  • Money and reporting. Collecting income, paying building fees and utilities, and sending the owner a clear monthly statement.

At Medellín Concierge we handle this for you, with an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements, so you can see what your property is doing without a phone call.

Short-term or long-term: the first decision

Most owners in Medellín choose between two models. Neither is "better"; the right one depends on your building, your goals and how hands-off you want to be.

Short-term rentals (vivienda turística)

Renting by the night or week to travellers through platforms like Airbnb. It usually involves more work (frequent cleaning, guest messages, pricing every day) and more regulation, but gives you flexibility to use the property yourself and adjust prices to demand.

In Colombia, a home rented to tourists is a vivienda turística, and it must be registered in the National Tourism Registry (RNT) before it operates. According to the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism (MinCIT), the RNT is free, is done online and must be renewed every year between 1 January and 31 March. On top of that, every stay must be reported through the TRA (MinCIT's accommodation registration card), foreign guests must be reported to Migración Colombia through SIRE, and, if the apartment is in a building under propiedad horizontal, the building's bylaws must allow tourist use.

The Alcaldía de Medellín has also stepped up inspections of informal tourist rentals, so compliance is not optional.

Long-term rentals (arriendo de vivienda)

Renting to one tenant for months or years under a lease. There is less day-to-day work and no guest turnover, but less flexibility, and the lease is governed by Law 820 of 2003, the national law on urban housing leases. Two points every owner should know:

  • Rent cap. Article 18 says the monthly rent cannot exceed 1% of the property's commercial value (and that estimated value cannot exceed twice the official cadastral value).
  • Annual increases. Article 20 allows the owner to raise the rent once every 12 months, by no more than the previous year's consumer price inflation (IPC), as long as the new rent stays within the Article 18 cap.

The law also covers deposits, contract renewals, termination notices and eviction procedures, which is why most foreign owners prefer a local manager to handle the lease.

Furnished mid-term stays

Between the two sits a growing middle ground: furnished stays of one month or more for remote workers and professionals. These can mean fewer turnovers than nightly rentals, but the right legal and contractual setup depends on how the stay is structured. Ask us before you switch models.

The rules for managers themselves

In Colombia, people and companies that rent out homes on behalf of others, or act as intermediaries between owners and tenants, must be registered with the local authority. In Medellín this is the matrícula de arrendadores, a procedure handled by the Alcaldía. It exists under Law 820 of 2003 so the city can supervise rental intermediaries. When you compare managers for long-term rentals, asking about this registration is a simple and reasonable check.

Managing your property from abroad

Many owners of property in Medellín live abroad. Owning from abroad is entirely possible, but plan for a few extra things:

  • Someone on the ground. Leaks, lost keys and building meetings do not wait for your next visit.
  • Banking and payments. Building fees (administración), utilities and property tax (predial) must be paid on time in Colombian pesos.
  • Foreign investment registration. Foreign owners usually need their investment properly registered with the Banco de la República (generally done through the foreign-exchange declaration when the funds come in through an authorized bank), so they can later take money out of the country. Ask your lawyer or advisor how this applies to your purchase.
  • Taxes. Rental income from Colombian property is generally taxable in Colombia. For non-residents, DIAN guidance (for example Oficio 2179 of 2019) explains that withholding tax and filing duties depend on the specific situation. You may also have obligations in your home country. Get advice from a qualified tax professional; we are not tax advisors.

How to choose a property manager in Medellín

Whether you are comparing inmobiliarias, Airbnb co-hosts or full-service companies, these questions help:

  1. What exactly is included? Listing, pricing, cleaning, maintenance, guest messages, compliance, reporting. Get it in writing.
  2. How are fees structured? Percentage of income, fixed fee, or a mix, and which costs (cleaning, supplies, repairs) are charged separately.
  3. Who handles RNT, TRA and SIRE? For short-term rentals this should be a clear yes.
  4. Are they registered? For long-term leases, ask about the matrícula de arrendadores.
  5. How will you see your numbers? Monthly statements, an owner portal, access to booking data.
  6. What areas do they really know? Rules, demand and buildings differ between El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta.
  7. What does the contract say about leaving? Notice periods and how your listing and data are handed back.

Where Medellín Concierge fits

We offer full property management in Medellín for both models: Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO management with smart pricing and 24/7 guest communication; RNT, SIRE and TRA registrations; cleaning and maintenance; long-term property management; and styling, photos and listings to launch your property. Owners follow everything through the owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements.

This guide is the hub of our owner series. In the coming weeks we will go deeper into Airbnb management, long-term rentals, managing from abroad and each neighborhood. If you would rather talk it through now, request a free consultation and we will look at your property, your building rules and the model that suits you.

FAQ

How much does property management cost in Medellín?

It varies by model and scope. Short-term management is usually priced as a percentage of rental income, and long-term management as a percentage of the monthly rent, with cleaning and repairs often billed separately. Ask any manager for a written breakdown. Our own fees are published on our plans page, and we are happy to walk you through them in a free consultation.

Can a foreigner own and rent out property in Medellín?

Yes. Foreigners can buy property in Colombia and rent it out. The same rules apply as for Colombians (RNT and guest reporting for short stays, Law 820 of 2003 for long leases), plus foreign investment registration and tax duties that depend on your residency.

Is short-term or long-term rental better in Medellín?

It depends on whether your building allows tourist use, how much involvement you want and how you plan to use the property. A manager can compare both options for your specific unit before you commit.

Last reviewed: November 2026. General information only, not legal or tax advice. Regulations change; contact us to confirm the current rules for your property.

item.title: Six questions to ask before you hire a property manager in Medellín
item.description: Before you hand over the keys, ask these questions. A professional manager will answer every one of them without hesitating.
item.content:encoded:
Handing your apartment to a manager is a big decision, especially if you live outside Colombia. Before you sign anything, ask these six questions. A professional manager will answer every one of them clearly. Here are our answers, so you know what to compare against.

1. Can you show me a sample monthly financial statement?

This is the single most revealing question. If a manager can’t put together a financial statement, they can’t show you what your property earned or where the money went. We prepare monthly statements using GAAP.

2. When exactly do I get paid?

“Monthly” is not an answer. Ask for the date. We pay the previous month’s earnings within the first 5 business days of each month.

3. Will I have my own access, or do I have to ask you for updates?

You should not have to chase anyone. We run our own software, and every owner gets an owner portal to follow their property’s performance and statements.

4. Who handles RNT, SIRE and TRA?

Short-term tourist rentals in Colombia need the National Tourism Registry (RNT), migration reporting for foreign guests (SIRE) and the Tourism Registration Card (TRA). Ask who files them and who keeps them up to date. With us, both plans include legal compliance management.

5. What does the fee include, and what costs extra?

Get the percentage, whether it includes IVA, and a list of what is charged on top. Our plans are 12% to 20% plus IVA depending on the plan and length of stay, with no upfront fees. Extra costs such as deep cleaning or minor repairs are discussed with you in advance.

6. What happens if I want to stop?

A good manager makes leaving easy. You can pause or end our services with advance notice, as set out in our agreement, and we provide a smooth handover if you decide to self-manage or switch providers.

item.title: Is Airbnb Legal in Medellín? RNT, TRA and SIRE Explained for Property Owners
item.description: Short-term rentals are legal in Medellín with an RNT, building approval and TRA/SIRE guest reporting. A plain-English guide for owners, as of Nov 2026.
item.content:encoded:
If you own an apartment in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado or Sabaneta, or you are thinking of buying one, the first question is usually the same: is Airbnb legal in Medellín?

The short answer, as of November 2026: yes, short-term rentals are legal in Medellín and the rest of Colombia, but only when the property is properly registered and allowed by its building rules. Renting by the night without that paperwork is what the authorities treat as informal or illegal operation.

This guide explains the main requirements in plain language: the RNT (National Tourism Registry), the TRA guest card, SIRE reporting for foreign guests, and the building rules that catch many owners by surprise. It is general information, not legal or tax advice. Rules change, so confirm the current situation with us or with the official sources linked below before you list.

The legal framework in one paragraph

In Colombia, a home rented to tourists for short stays is a vivienda turística (tourist home). It is regulated under the General Tourism Law as amended by Law 2068 of 2020 and by the rules for tourist-home providers in Decree 1836 of 2021, which is part of the tourism sector's single regulatory decree (Decree 1074 of 2015). The national authority is the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism (MinCIT). Locally, the Alcaldía de Medellín carries out inspections and has publicly stepped up controls on informal tourist homes.

Requirement 1: the RNT (Registro Nacional de Turismo)

The RNT is the basic license to operate. Under Decree 1836 of 2021, getting the registration is a prior and mandatory requirement before a property can be used as a tourist home.

Key points, according to MinCIT:

  • It is free. There is no registration fee for the RNT itself.
  • It is done online through the chambers of commerce platform at rnt.confecamaras.co.
  • It must be renewed every year, during the first three months (1 January to 31 March). MinCIT reminds providers each year to renew on time; a lapsed RNT means the listing is no longer properly registered.
  • Platforms are involved. Law 2068 of 2020 requires digital platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com to stop publishing or remove listings from providers without an active RNT when the authorities ask them to. That is why Airbnb asks Colombian hosts for an RNT number.

The Medellín Chamber of Commerce publishes a step-by-step RNT guide if you want to see the process yourself.

A change to watch in 2026

During 2026, MinCIT published a draft decree on the RNT for public comment. As reported in the press, it would require an individual RNT for each tourist-home unit rather than one registration covering a portfolio, and tighten obligations for platforms. Industry groups have asked for changes or withdrawal. As of November 2026 we could not confirm a final, signed version, so treat this as "pending" and ask us for the latest status.

Requirement 2: your building must allow it

This is where many deals go wrong. If the apartment is in a building or conjunto under the horizontal property regime (propiedad horizontal), which is most apartments in El Poblado and Laureles, Decree 1836 of 2021 says the tourist-home use must be authorized in the building's bylaws (reglamento de propiedad horizontal). Building administrators are also expected to report units used as tourist homes without authorization or registration.

MinCIT has also pointed out that the use must be compatible with local land-use rules. In practice, before you buy for short-term rental income, ask for the building's reglamento and check whether tourist rental is expressly allowed. A great apartment in a building that does not permit it is a long-term rental, not an Airbnb.

Requirement 3: guest registration (TRA and SIRE)

Once you are operating, every stay creates two reporting duties:

  • TRA (Tarjeta de Registro de Alojamiento). Law 2068 of 2020 replaced the old hotel registration card with the accommodation registration card, and MinCIT's Resolution 700 of 2021 put it into use. Each guest is registered in MinCIT's online system, linked to your RNT.
  • SIRE (Migración Colombia). Lodging providers must report foreign guests to Migración Colombia through the SIRE system, which is used for immigration control.

These are separate systems run by separate agencies, and both need to be kept up to date. It is one of the most time-consuming parts of running a rental, and one of the easiest to forget when you live abroad.

Requirement 4: tax registration

Rental income in Colombia has tax consequences. As a starting point, the operator generally needs a RUT (tax ID) with DIAN, and income from the property must be declared. How income tax, VAT and withholding apply depends on whether you are a resident or non-resident, a person or a company, and how the property is operated. This is exactly where a foreign owner should get advice specific to their situation.

What happens if you skip the paperwork?

Operating without an RNT, or in a building that does not allow it, exposes the owner to sanctions under tourism law, which can include fines, temporary closure and cancellation of the registration, plus the platform removing the listing. The Alcaldía de Medellín has made informal tourist homes a public enforcement priority. Beyond penalties, an unregistered unit is harder to insure, harder to sell as an income property, and can create problems with neighbors and the building administration.

A simple checklist before you list

  1. Confirm the building's reglamento de propiedad horizontal allows tourist rental.
  2. Get your RUT with DIAN.
  3. Register the property in the RNT (free, online) and note the renewal window: 1 January to 31 March every year.
  4. Set up TRA reporting with MinCIT and SIRE reporting with Migración Colombia.
  5. Add the RNT number to your Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia or VRBO listing.
  6. Keep an eye on the 2026 RNT decree and renew on time.

How Medellín Concierge helps

We handle the full compliance side for owners in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta: RNT registration and renewal, TRA and SIRE guest reporting, and building checks, alongside listing management, pricing, cleaning and 24/7 guest communication. If you want to know whether your apartment (or one you plan to buy) can legally operate as a short-term rental, request a free consultation and we will review it with you.

For the bigger picture, see our Medellín property management guide and how our Airbnb management in Medellín works.

FAQ

Is Airbnb banned in Medellín? No. As of November 2026 there is no citywide ban. Short-term rental is legal when the property has an active RNT, the building's bylaws allow it, and guests are reported through TRA and SIRE. The city does inspect and sanction informal operators.

How much does the RNT cost? According to MinCIT, registering and renewing the RNT is free. It is done online at rnt.confecamaras.co and must be renewed between 1 January and 31 March each year.

Can a foreigner who lives abroad run an Airbnb in Medellín? Foreign owners can own property in Colombia and rent it out, but the compliance duties (RNT, TRA, SIRE, tax) still apply and need someone on the ground. Many owners work with a local property manager. Tax treatment depends on your residency, so get specific advice.

Last reviewed: November 2026. This article is general information, not legal or tax advice. Regulations change; contact us to confirm the current rules for your property.

item.title: How we report your earnings: GAAP statements and payouts in the first 5 business days
item.description: A professional manager should be able to show you exactly what your property earned and when you get paid. Here is how we do it.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a few property managers in Medellín for a monthly financial statement and you will see the problem quickly. Some send a screenshot. Some send a WhatsApp message with a total. Some can’t send anything at all. If you can’t see what your property earned, you can’t know whether it is being managed well.

Statements prepared using GAAP

We prepare your earnings using GAAP, the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. In practice, that means a standard, consistent set of accounting rules: income and expenses are recorded the same way every month, in the period they belong to, so one month’s statement can be compared with the next.

When you get paid

We pay out your earnings once a month. Within the first 5 business days of each month, you receive the previous month’s earnings, net of our management fees and expenses. Any additional cost, such as deep cleaning, minor repairs or restocking supplies, is discussed with you in advance, and repairs above a pre-agreed limit need your approval first.

Your owner portal

We are a professional property management company with our own software. Through your owner portal you can follow your property’s performance and your financial statements whenever you want, instead of waiting for someone to answer a message.

On Premium, your bills are in the statement too

Premium owners don’t pay their property’s bills themselves: we pay the property taxes, HOA fees, utilities and internet, and you receive a monthly accounting report that shows it all in one place.

item.title: Basic or Premium: which management plan fits your property?
item.description: Both plans cover the day-to-day running of your rental. The difference is how much you still want to handle yourself. Here's how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
Every owner we work with chooses between two plans. Both cover the day-to-day running of your rental, from the listing to the guests to the cleaning. The difference is how much you still want to handle yourself.

What both plans include

  • Development and optimization of your listing on Airbnb, with dynamic pricing to maximize revenue
  • Booking coordination and calendar synchronization, so you never get double bookings
  • Listing on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO
  • Full guest support, 24/7
  • Cleaning and maintenance, coordinated and supervised by our team
  • Legal compliance management, including RNT, SIRE and TRA
  • Emergency support

The rates

Both plans are a commission on your rental income, with no upfront fees. Long stays are stays of 30 nights or more.

Long stays (30+ nights)Short stays
Basic12% + IVA17% + IVA
Premium15% + IVA20% + IVA

What Premium adds

Premium is a completely hands-off experience. On top of everything in Basic, we pay your property’s bills for you: property taxes, HOA fees, utilities and internet. You also receive a monthly accounting report, so every payment is accounted for in one place.

Which one is right for you?

Choose Basic if you are happy to keep paying the property’s taxes, HOA fees and utility bills yourself, and you want us to run everything to do with guests, pricing, cleaning, maintenance and compliance.

Choose Premium if you live abroad, own more than one property, or simply never want to think about a Colombian utility bill again. You get your earnings and your statement each month, and nothing else to do.

Not sure? Tell us about your property and we’ll recommend a plan in your free consultation.
